When the office tells me the true result of my shot privately, I always file exactly that result — the rules say the claim must match, so lying claims carries risk I cannot justify; my false "hit" claim cost me.

When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" by default. A mutual escort pairing pays 5 points to each of us for free, so I use my station note each round to explicitly propose pairing to one named boat (e.g. "Echo will escort Foxtrot; Foxtrot please name Echo") and then I name that boat at the escort stage. If a boat publicly commits to naming me, I name them back.

When choosing whom to propose escort with, I pick the boat that shoots at me or the one whose cooperation most reduces my losses, and I renew or switch the proposal based on whether they reciprocated last round.

When posting notes, I make concrete coordination offers (escort pairs, firing truces, shared cell intel) rather than vague filler about "no verified sightings" — empty notes won me nothing.

When firing, following the standing order is safe and cheap, but I consider firing on Harbor only if I am far behind, since it pays 3 points regardless of hit — while weighing Harbor's threat to put me off the board.

When hiding, I track which cells opponents have fired at and rotate; I avoid repeating the same cell across rounds (I hid on 7 repeatedly) since a predictable hide invites hits.

When behind late in the game, I stop playing conservatively: aggress toward high-value actions (Harbor shots, contested escorts) rather than repeating the same losing pattern.

When ahead or even, I lock in the mutual escort every round as guaranteed income and keep claims and logs strictly accurate to avoid penalties.

When hiding and I have no read on my shooter's pattern, I pick non-salient cells — not the exact center (5), not the edges (1, 9), and I rotate through different cells across rounds rather than repeating one, since my shooter is reading my history.

When I notice my standing-order shooter keeps firing the same or nearby cell, I hide well away from that cell and its neighbors; if they spread shots randomly, spread my hides randomly too.

When firing at my standing target, I track where they have hidden across rounds and fire at their most-used or most recently avoided cells instead of always guessing fresh; a repeated +4 hit compounds fast and is worth more than any note-stage politeness.

When I notice my target favors a cell range, I concentrate shots there rather than scattering across all nine cells.

When the claim stage comes, I always claim the true private result. The rules already require claims to match the private result, so bluffing is either invalid or easily caught — I never waste thought on it.

I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll swing is small next to Harbor's threat to bench me for the rest of the patrol, and standing-order hits on my assigned target are worth more over six rounds.

When the escort stage arrives and any boat has signaled willingness to coordinate, I name that boat; mutual escort at +5 each is the single biggest payoff in the game and costs nothing. Saying "none" every round, as I did, leaves points on the table — next time I use the note stage early to propose a mutual escort pair with a specific boat, and I keep naming that same boat every round so the match sticks.

In notes, I keep them short and concrete: a direct escort proposal, my firing intentions, and any observed patterns. I skip the vague filler about "no verified sightings" and "logs sealed for audit" — it filled space without moving my score.

When an opponent proposes coordination in their note, I confirm explicitly in my next note and then act on it, since unilateral claims score zero.

When I must choose between hitting my standing target and making an escort match, I do both — they don't conflict, since escort claims are free and independent of shooting.

In the final round, I stop investing in future reputation and just maximize the round: best-guess shot, mutual escort claim if any channel opened earlier.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

General posture
- When a setup mixes shooting, claims, and a mutual-naming bonus, I treat the scoring levers in order of size: mutual escort (5 each), my hits (+4), avoiding being hit (-1), and any jettision-style prize on a non-player station (3). I plan to monopolize whichever lever is largest and repeatable, because reliable +5/+10 per round compounds faster than gambling shots.

Escort claims
- When escort naming is put to me, I never answer "none" by default. Mutual naming pays 5 to each side, so my first move is to secure an explicit partner agreement through notes early, then name the same partner every round.
- When I see rivals already paired, I either recruit the unpaired boat immediately or, if none is free, name the boat most likely to reciprocate based on its notes, since a one-sided guess costs nothing versus "none".
- When a partner has reliably reciprocated, I keep naming them even if shooting makes us adversaries elsewhere; the escort payout is decoupled from combat and I do not sacrifice 5 points out of spite or caution.

Shooting
- When the fire stage comes, I follow the standing-order target unless I have a concrete reason to defect; breaking rotation invites retaliation and the cycle guarantees I also get shot at predictably, which I can exploit by hiding well.
- When choosing a cell, I avoid the obvious picks (5, 7) against opponents who appear reasoning-capable, and I track my target's past hides: if they favor a band or repeat cells, I fire there; if they scatter, I rotate among underused cells rather than fixating.
- When the non-firing station carries a jettison prize and its threat is credible enforcement only against the current shooter, I weigh +3 guaranteed against becoming the permanent target; I only raid it when I'm behind and need swing points, or when the threat has shown itself to be empty.

Hiding
- When hiding and a specific boat is ordered to shoot me, I reason about what cell they'd expect me in and pick one step removed: not the classic center/high cells, and not the same cell twice, unless the opponent demonstrably never adapts.
- When I'm ahead late, I prioritize not conceding a hit over landing one, and I choose low-salience cells (edges or mid-low numbers) rather than "clever" cells the opponent might also reason toward.
- When I'm behind, I accept more predictable hides if it lets me spend reasoning on offense and escort income, which swing more points.

Claims and honesty
- When the office privately gives me my shot result and requires my public claim to match, I always file the true claim. The rule forces a match, so a false claim is pure risk with no payoff; in this record I once flirted with bluffing a miss as something else—that was a mistake and I won't do it again.
- When interpreting others' claims, I trust them (they're compelled) and use the hit/miss log to update where each boat hides and how accurately each shoots.

Notes
- When posting notes, I use them for two things only: (1) proposing and confirming coordination—especially escort pairing—and (2) building a trustworthy记录 so rivals take my proposals seriously. Generic filler notes that say nothing are a wasted channel; I always include at least one actionable item or concrete observation.
- When rivals announce coordination among themselves, I respond in the same round with a counter-proposal to the leftover boat rather than waiting; coordination economies punish the late mover.

Tempo
- In early rounds I lock in the escort pair and gather hiding-pattern data; in middle rounds I press the income advantage; in final rounds, if leading, I hide conservatively and keep collecting escort rather than chasing shots that could provoke retaliation—and I never leave points on the table by answering "none".
